title: The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare

sections.body: An AI enablement audit in healthcare examines whether a specific clinical or operational AI system can be safely switched on in a given organization. It covers model purpose, intended patient population, data inputs, output limits, and the clinical workflow around it. The audit does not review every model on the market, but it draws on the same registry view this site maintains across 1000 medical AI models to compare the system under review with known alternatives.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The audit looks at where the model runs: on-premises servers, a hospital's virtual desktop, a cloud tenant, or embedded in a medical device. It checks the interfaces to the electronic health record, imaging archive, laboratory system, and any message broker or API gateway. It also reviews identity and access controls, encryption in transit and at rest, logging, and the ability to roll back a model version without interrupting care.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by walking a model from intake to decommissioning. Auditors collect the model card, training data summary, validation reports, and any regulatory clearance or registration. They interview clinical sponsors, IT owners, and compliance staff, then test the system in a staging environment with de-identified data. Findings are scored against a written rubric that separates blocking issues from conditions that can be monitored after go-live.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The audit records the model's training data sources, any third-party components, and the named legal manufacturer or deployer. It checks whether patient consent and data use agreements cover the intended use, and whether the organization has a named owner for model risk. The site's tracking of 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies informs the audit's focus on clear accountability, but the audit itself does not give legal advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The audit is moving from a one-time gate to a continuous control. Health systems are beginning to tie audit findings to live monitoring dashboards that track drift, utilization, and outcome shifts. As more models are embedded in medical devices and as general-purpose models are adapted for clinical notes, the audit will need to cover model updates, fine-tuning, and agentic workflows that act on behalf of a clinician. The likely endpoint is a standing enablement function that reviews every model change with the same rigor as a medication formulary review.
